rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an uses barūz for forceful manifestation at resurrection and judgment, as in the cited scenes of people appearing before God.
rows.anchor: والقرآن يستعمل البروز، وهو قوة الشخوص والظهور، في موقف القيامة والحساب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Jahīm names a fiercely blazing fire; the religious term preserves its lexical sense of intense ignition.
rows.anchor: فالجحيم والجحمة في اللغة: النار الشديدة التأجج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive construction suppresses the agent, foregrounding Hell’s appearing and the event’s apparent agency.
rows.anchor: وإسناد البروز إلى الجحيم، بالبناء للمجهول، تطرد به الظاهرة الأسلوبية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Athara means a remaining trace or legacy, and here preferring worldly life evokes what one chooses to retain or leave behind.
rows.anchor: الأثر، لغة: بقية الشيء، ومنه الخبر المأثور الباقي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’anic āwā can mean granting refuge and can also describe hoped-for or imagined refuge, as the cited examples show.
rows.anchor: وإما على سبيل الرجاء أو الوهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fearing one’s Lord’s standing evokes continual awareness of standing before God, whether maqām is read as an action, time, or place.
rows.anchor: في ذكر المقام هنا، مقام ربه، إيحاء بأن الخائف يراقب ربه في كل عمله ومسعاه

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says attaching maqām to the Lord magnifies the station and inspires profound awe.
rows.anchor: وفي إضافة المقام للرب تفخيم للمقام وتهويل عظيم واقع من النفوس موقعاً عظيماً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hawā means inclination, originally likened to a raptor plunging on prey; it may draw toward good or evil, though usage is mostly blameworthy.
rows.anchor: والهوى الميل، وربما كان أصل استعماله في: هوت العقاب إذا انقضت على فريستها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’anic examples associate following hawā with misguidance, supporting the reading here as surrender to ruinous desire.
rows.anchor: وهذا التتبع، يؤيد ما يطمئن به السياق في آية النازعات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nahā also evokes reason and sound judgment, so restraining the self from desire answers the voice of intellect.
rows.anchor: فكما استعملت العربية ضد الأمر، استعملت "النَهَى" كذلك في العقل والرشد، ومنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s warning has reached its culmination, then it settles the question of the Hour by saying its final knowledge belongs to God.
rows.anchor: لا يدع الموقف دون أن يعقب عليه بحسم عقدته، والرد على سؤالهم عن الساعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Arabic, sāʿah first denotes a portion of time, later conventionally specified as sixty minutes; the Qur’anic eschatological usage is distinctive.
rows.anchor: ولفظ الساعة في العربية، يعني الجزء من الوقت، ثم تحدد. بستين دقيقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When indefinite, sāʿah in the Qur’an denotes a short, unspecified span, while the definite Hour consistently means the Afterlife’s decisive event.
rows.anchor: أما حين يستعمل القرآن "الساعة" معرفة بـ: ال، فتلك - دائماً - هي ساعة الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Hour is presented as active and momentous through verbs of coming and rising, marking the change in cosmic order.
rows.anchor: أن هذه "الساعة" تنفرد دون ساعات الزمان كله، بأنها الحاسمة الفاصلة التي يتغير فيها نظام الزمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ordinary Arabic, the definite sāʿah can mean the present moment; later the word also named the timekeeping instrument.
rows.anchor: ويستعمل معرفا بـ (ال) للعهد، ظرف زمان للوقت الحاضر، فيقال: أزورك الساعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an deliberately redirects questions about the Hour’s time and place because God alone knows it; fronting the phrase restricts its endpoint to Him.
rows.anchor: على وجه القصر الصريح بالتقديم والتأخير في الآية: {إِلَى رَبِّكَ مُنْتَهَاهَا} لا إلى غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone knows the Hour, and to Him alone it returns; its knowledge has not been granted to any created being.
rows.anchor: عنده وحده علم الساعة، وإليه وحده مردها ومنهاها، ففيم أنت من ذكراها يا محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s task concerning the Hour is restricted to warning those who fear it, not announcing its time or place; Abū Ḥayyān says warning benefits such people.
rows.anchor: فيه قصر لمهمة النبي عليه الصلاوة والسلام، فيما يتعلق بهذه الساعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khashya is fear joined with reverence for the feared one, most often attributed in the Qur’an to believers, messengers, scholars, and those hoped to be guided.
rows.anchor: والخشية ليست مجرد خوف، وإنما هي خوف مشوب برهبة المخشي وإعظامه

none: The segment is only the complete surah text, with no commentary.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Restricting the unnamed father to Muhammad, Noah, or Abraham undermines the generality of the indefinite noun and the nonhuman-inclusive wording mā walad.
rows.anchor: وتخصيص والد، بمحمد - صلى الله عليه وسلم -، أو نوح، أو إبراهيم، عليهما السلام، يبعده

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abū Zayd, as transmitted by Abū Ḥayyān, identifies al-insān as Adam.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو زيد فيما نقل أبو حيان: إن الإنسان هو آدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’anic usage makes al-insān a morally responsible human being who speaks, disputes, bears trusts and duties, and is tested by good and evil.
rows.anchor: فالإنسان هو الذي يختص بالبيان والجدل ويحتمل التكليف والأمانة والعهد والوصية، والإبتلاء بالخير والشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kabad appears nowhere else in the Qur’an; its lexical path moves from liver pain to hardship and endured suffering.
rows.anchor: وأصل الكبد في اللغة من وجع الكبد، يقال: كبد الرجل يكبده، ضرب كبده

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the verse describes sick hearts and corrupt inner nature, then limits it to those God knew would disbelieve; the author contrasts this with a generic reading.
rows.anchor: فالزمخشري يقول: "لقد خلقنا الإنسان في مرض هو مرض القلب وفساد الباطن"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author allows the hardship interpretations but questions how the preceding oath about the city and generations connects to them.
rows.anchor: وكل ذلك يمكن أن يقال، لكن ما وجه ارتباط القسم بهذا البلد، ووالد وما ولد، بتلك الشدة التي خلق فيها الإنسان

rows.speaker: محمد عبده
rows.claim: Muhammad ʿAbduh says humanity is made for toil because people are parents and offspring, each bearing the difficulties of growth.
rows.anchor: إن الإنسان نوع من الوالد والمولود، فحق له أن يخلق في كبد وكد ونصب

rows.speaker: محمد عبده
rows.claim: Muhammad ʿAbduh presents the Prophet’s mistreatment as part of the human burden borne by every child of humanity.
rows.anchor: وما يصيب الرسول من تقريع المستحلين لحرمته، فهو من شأن الإنسان وقدر قدر على كل مولود منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author notes that Muhammad ʿAbduh extends mā walad to every offspring of humans, animals, and plants, and questions whether their hardships equal the burden of prophethood.
rows.anchor: فجعل {مَا وَلَدَ} في ألاية، لكل مولود من إنسان وحيوان ونبات

rows.speaker: التبيان
rows.claim: Al-Tibyān says no creature undergoes what Adam’s descendants endure: the afflictions of this world and the hardships of the next.
rows.anchor: لم يخلق الله خلقاً يكابد ما يكابد إبن آدم

rows.speaker: إبن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains kabad as hardship through conception, birth, nursing, growth, livelihood, life, and death.
rows.anchor: يعني بالكبد، حمله وولادته ورضاعه وفصاله

rows.speaker: إبن القيم
rows.claim: Ibn al-Qayyim traces human struggle from womb and infancy through responsibility, livelihood, death, the grave, judgment, and punishment, with rest in Paradise.
rows.anchor: الإنسان مخلوق في شدة، بكون في الرحم ثم في القماط ثم في الرباط

rows.speaker: محمد عبده
rows.claim: Muhammad ʿAbduh reads the hardship as labor in using one’s faculties, eating and drinking, and protecting one’s family.
rows.anchor: إنه في عناء من تصريف قواه في عمله، بل وفي أكله وشربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author questions these readings’ connection to the oath and rejects equating the burden of prophethood with ordinary growth and development.
rows.anchor: ووجه الغرابة في هذا التأويل أن يسوى بين أعباء الرسالة، وما يتحمله كل مولود من عناء النمو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kabad is the innate human capacity to bear moral responsibility and the hard choice between good and evil, fitting Mecca’s mistreatment of the Prophet and the verses that follow.
rows.anchor: احتمال المسئولية ومشقة الاختيار بين الخير والشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Using khalaqnā rather than jaʿalnā signals that humans are created by nature for this struggle of responsibility, moral testing, and accountability.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى أن الإنسان مخلوق بفطرته لهذه المكابدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question portrays a powerful, wealthy person’s conceit that no one can overpower him; its compressed, sudden form both asserts and condemns that delusion, with lan intensifying its denial.
rows.anchor: وبلاغة الاستفهام في الآية، تأتي من هذا الطى المتعمد لتحديد نوع الكبد

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī treats lā as semantically repeated: the verse means the person neither climbed the obstacle nor believed.
rows.anchor: هي متكررة في المعنى، على تقدير: فلا اقتحم العقبة ولا آمن

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj derives an implicit negation of faith from the later phrase thumma kāna min alladhīna āmanū.
rows.anchor: وعند الزجاج أن قوله تعالى: {ثُمَّ كَانَ مِنَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا} يدل على معنى: فلا اقتحم العقبة، ولا آمن

rows.speaker: محمد عبده
rows.claim: Muhammad ʿAbduh rejects these emendations because classical Arabic can use lā with a past verb without repetition and the Qur’an is eloquent proof.
rows.anchor: لأن القرآن حجة في الفصاحة، وقد ورد في كلامهم عدم تكرارها

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes lā interrogative, or treats it as a shortened form of the exhortative alā; some, including Muhammad ʿAbduh, reject the latter as unattested.
rows.anchor: وقريب منه القول بأن (لا) في الآية من: (ألا) التي للتحضيض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whichever construction is chosen, the phrase conveys censure and exhortation; negation and rhetorical question converge, while lā directly denies that the deluded person climbed the obstacle.
rows.anchor: تشعر بالإنكار والتأنيب والحض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ links creation for moral struggle and the gift of discernment to the charge to climb the demanding obstacle.
rows.anchor: والفاء هنا، للربط والترتيب: خلق الإنسان مهيئاً لمكابدة المسئولية

rows.speaker: الحسن البصري
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī says the difficult obstacle is the struggle against oneself, its desires, and Satan, as cited by al-Ṭabarī.
rows.anchor: في الطبري عن الحسن البصري: عقبة والله شديدة. مجاهدة الإنسان نفسه وهواه وعدوه الشيطان

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī offers a reading close to al-Ḥasan’s account of the obstacle as moral struggle.
rows.anchor: وقريب منه، ما قاله الزمخشري، ونقله الشيخ محمد عبده

rows.speaker: الحسن، إبن عباس، مجاهد، كعب
rows.claim: A second transmitted view identifies the obstacle as Hell or a mountain within it, escaped only through good deeds; Abū Ḥayyān attributes it to these authorities.
rows.anchor: وعن إبن عباس ومجاهد وكعب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the need for allegorical explanations because the Qur’an itself answers its question by defining the obstacle through emancipation, feeding, faith, patience, and mercy.
rows.anchor: ونرى السياق في غير حاجة إلى تأويل يغنى عنه أن القرآن نفسه قد تول بيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah presents the obstacle as a diagnosis of unjust conditions produced by powerful owners’ arrogance and tyranny.
rows.anchor: بيان لأوضاع ظالمة نشأت عن غرور القادرين وطغيان أصحاب المال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence makes freeing an enslaved person the first step toward human dignity; broader social reform follows only after slavery’s dehumanizing injury is repaired.
rows.anchor: تحرير الإنسانية من أغلال الرق هو أول خطوة في النضال الصعب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Returning to sound nature reveals the clarity of good and evil, human weakness before the Creator, and accountability for injustices in Mecca.
rows.anchor: ولو أن هذا الإنسان قد رجع إلى فطرته، وثاب إلى رشده وحسه وبصيرته، لاهتدى إلى معالم الخير والشر واضحة أمامه شاخصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author portrays Meccan injustice as desecrating the Prophet’s sanctuary while powerful owners enslave people and leave relatives and the poor hungry.
rows.anchor: وأي شر أفدح وأوضح، من أن يستحل أذى الرسول في البلد الحرام؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah calls people to struggle against slavery, class divisions, and social oppression by appealing to their innate capacity for moral effort.
rows.anchor: القرآن إذ يدعو هنا إلى المجاهدة ضد الرق، والفروق الطبقية والظلم الإجتماعي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Masghabah is famine or widespread hunger; depicting a day of famine heightens the horror of a needy neighbor going unfed, as Abū Ḥayyān also says.
rows.anchor: فالمسغبة المجاعة، أو هو الجوع العام كما قال "أو حيان"، وليس أبشع من تصور جار يتيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An orphan described as dhā maqrabah may be near in place or related by kinship, and either relation entails the rights of proximity and family.
rows.anchor: وكون اليتيم ذا مقربة، يفسر بالقرب وبالقرابة، ولكليهما حق الجوار والقربى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A miskīn with matrabah is in extreme want, lying in the dust or having nothing but dust.
rows.anchor: يلصق المسكين بالتراب، أو يجعله، من فرط العدم، لا يجد سوى التراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author takes thumma as real sequence: restoring dignity through emancipation and social justice through feeding are prerequisites for faith and its mutual exhortations.
rows.anchor: عطف الإيمان، بلفظ: ثم، على ما قبله يبيح لنا أن نفهم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī reads thumma as distance in virtue and rank, not time, since faith precedes and validates good works.
rows.anchor: وجاء بثم لتراخي الإيمان وتباعده في الفضيلة والرتبة عن العتق والصدقة

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān proposes rank rather than temporal delay because faith must precede valid deeds, or that the phrase describes dying in faith, or merely delayed mention.
rows.anchor: ثم، لتراخي الإيمان والفضيلة لا للتراخي في الزمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects readings that detach faith from emancipation and feeding, arguing genuine faith requires resistance to tyranny, enslavement, and indifference to the poor.
rows.anchor: لكن المفسرين عطلوا هذا الملحظ الجليل، بل عكسوا الوضع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The order makes human dignity and social justice grounds of faith; a society that accepts human enslavement and starvation cannot sustain sincere faith.
rows.anchor: معلناً أن لا مكان لإيمان صادق مخلص، في مجتمع يسيغ عبودية بشر لغير خالقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conjunction waw links faith directly with mutual exhortation: sound faith brings patience in the struggle for good and merciful solidarity among people.
rows.anchor: عطف التواصي بالصبر والتواصي بالمرحمة على الإيمان بالواو المفيدة للربط دون تفاوت او تراخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ideal community speaks against injustice, since God gave people tongues and lips so they would not remain silent about truth.
rows.anchor: وقد جعل الله للإنسان لساناً وشفتين. كي لا يسكت عن الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The right side conventionally evokes blessing, good fortune, and strength; Qur’anic usage associates it with the blessed place where God addressed Moses.
rows.anchor: وقد ألفت العربية استعمال اليمين في البركة واليمن والتفاؤل والقوة

none: The segment is only the complete surah text, with no commentary.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Meccan surah is commonly dated as the sixteenth in revelation, after al-Kawthar; its concise, emphatic warning dominates its tone.
rows.anchor: السورة مكية بلا خلاف، وهي السادسة عشرة في ترتيب النزول، على المشهور

rows.speaker: النيسابوري
rows.claim: Al-Nīsābūrī links this surah to al-Qāriʿah; the author rejects a chronological link because Takāthur precedes it by thirteen surahs, while allowing a shared warning tone in the muṣḥaf arrangement.
rows.anchor: وقد ربطها بعض المفسرين - كالنيسابورى - بسورة القارعة

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī treats the opening as a reproachful question rather than a declarative sentence.
rows.anchor: لكن "الرازي" أخرجها من الإخبار إلى الاستفهام بمعنى التوبيخ والتقريع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The declarative reading warns more forcefully because it states that distraction by accumulation actually occurred, rather than asking whether it did.
rows.anchor: والخبرية هنا أوقع في الزجر وأبلغ في الوعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lahw means what distracts; its root may evoke the mill-hand’s handful that occupies the grinder and keeps it turning.
rows.anchor: واللهو لغة، ما يلهى الإنسان. ولعل أصل استعماله في اللهوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In al-Takāthur, the specific distraction is accumulation itself, from the root for abundance and increase.
rows.anchor: أن الإلهاء فيها بالتكاثر. وهو لغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an uses lahw for many kinds of futile distraction, including a person, money and children, trade, hopes, and speech.
rows.anchor: أو أموال وأولاد: {يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’anic coordination of play and lahw shows that a distraction need not be playful.
rows.anchor: وصنيع القرآن يؤذن بأن اللهو أيضاً قد يكون ليس بلعب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Takāthur derives from abundance and growth in quantity; abundance can figuratively suggest honor, unlike scarcity’s association with abasement.
rows.anchor: وهو لغة: تفاعل من الكثرة نقيض القلة، ونماء العدد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī conflates mutual boasting and accumulation, but the author rejects redundancy because the Qur’an coordinates takāthur separately from tafākhur.
rows.anchor: وجعل "الرازي" التفاخر والتكاثر شيئاً واحداً، وهو ما لا يوافق نسق آية الحديد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In al-Ḥadīd, takāthur means scrambling for worldly goods and seeking to monopolize them, a stage beyond frivolity, distraction, decoration, and boastful rivalry; al-Nīsābūrī also reports this view.
rows.anchor: وإنه التكالب على حطام الدنيا ومحاولة الاستئثار به

rows.speaker: جمهرة المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes understand takāthur as boasting and rivalry, influenced by reports about the occasion of revelation.
rows.anchor: وإن يكن جمهرة المفسرين أكثر ميلاً إلى عد التكاثر هنا مباهاة وتفاخراً

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says the verse concerns boasting over wealth and numbers; Qatādah reports clans claiming to outnumber one another.
rows.anchor: فالإمام الطبري ذهب إلى "أنها المباهاة بكثرة المال والعدد

rows.speaker: البحر المحيط
rows.claim: Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ reports that the verse was revealed concerning the Jews.
rows.anchor: وفي (البحر المحيط) أنها نزلت في اليهود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the verse leaves the object of accumulation unspecified, the author rejects restricting it to money, numbers, or the dead, and also rejects limiting its scope to blameworthy kinds by importing a restriction.
rows.anchor: ما ذهب الراغب، أو نقصره على العدد كما قال الرازي، أو الموتى كما في النيسابورى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address covers everyone distracted by accumulating worldly adornments such as wealth and children, whatever the specific reported occasion.
rows.anchor: والخطاب هنا عام لكل من ألهاهم التكاثر والتكالب على زينة الدنيا من مال وولد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥattā marks the endpoint: accumulation ends at the cemeteries, and the abrupt movement from rivalry to graves completes the warning.
rows.anchor: في: حتى، هنا معنى الغاية، فغاية التكاثر إلى زيادرة المقابر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an uses ziyārah only here and the related form tazāwar in al-Kahf; the root also denotes falsehood or deviation from truth.
rows.anchor: ولم يستعمل القرآن الزيارة إلا في آية التكاثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sensory root of z-w-r is inclination or curvature; its derivatives describe turning toward someone, a dream-vision, or deviation from truth.
rows.anchor: والدلالة الحسية لها في اللغة، الميل والاعوجاج

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: One interpretation takes the visit literally: people went to the graves to count their dead.
rows.anchor: إن الزيارة بمعناها الحقيقي، حين ذهب المتكاثرون إلى القبور يعدون موتاهم

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: A second interpretation treats visiting as metaphorical mention of dead ancestors while boasting; Abū Ḥayyān rejects it because the wording visit is awkward for that sense.
rows.anchor: هذا تعبير ينبو عنه لفظ: زرتم

rows.speaker: بنو سهم وبنو عبد مناف
rows.claim: A reported occasion says these clans competed over numbers, then counted their dead as well as the living after one claimed losses in pre-Islamic feuding.
rows.anchor: أن بني سهم وبني عبد مناف تفاخروا أيهم أكثر عدداً

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: A third interpretation takes visiting the graves as dying; al-Ṭabarī adopts it, citing familiar Arabic usage and poetry by Jarīr.
rows.anchor: والقول الثالث، إن الزيارة هنا معناها الموت، وهو استعمال مألوف في العربية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading grave-visiting as death implies a temporary stay: visitors leave, so the wording itself hints at resurrection, reckoning, and recompense.
rows.anchor: والزائر غير مقيم، وسوف تنتهي الزيارة حتماً إلى بعث وحساب وجزاء

rows.speaker: أعرابي
rows.claim: A Bedouin who heard the verse inferred resurrection, saying visitors depart rather than remain.
rows.anchor: بعث القوم للقيامة ورب الكعبة، فإن الزائر منصرف لا مقيم

rows.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز
rows.claim: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz is also reported to have expressed a view like the Bedouin’s insight.
rows.anchor: وروى كذلك هن "عمر بن عبد العزيز" نحو من قول الأعرابي

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān passes quickly over the Bedouin’s insight and instead cites a view that the verse rebukes boasting through repeated cemetery visits, distinguishing later permitted visits for admonition.
rows.anchor: إنه تأنيب على الإكثار من زيارة القبور تكثراً بمن سلف وإشادة بذكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Maqābir appears only in this verse, while qubūr appears five times and the singular qabr is used in al-Tawbah.
rows.anchor: ولفظ "المقابر" لم يأت في غير آية التكاثر، على حين جاءت "القبور" خمس مرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although maqābir suits takāthur in sound, its stronger reason is semantic: it evokes the vast collective cemetery across ages and classes, broader than individual graves.
rows.anchor: واستعمالها هنا يقتضيه معنوياً، أنه اللفظ الملائم للتكاثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reducing maqābir to a lexical synonym for graves misses its broad setting and the verse’s compressed journey from worldly rivalry to death.
rows.anchor: فتأويل المقابر بالقبور، لسي إلا أثراص مفردات القرآن تناولا لفظياً معجمياً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated threat is directed at those distracted by accumulation, and repetition intensifies the rebuke.
rows.anchor: واضح هنا أن الخطاب لمن الهالهم التكاثر، وأن التكرار مبالغة في الزجر

none: The segment is only the opening portion of the complete surah text, with no commentary.
The segment is only the continuation of the complete surah text, with no commentary.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is early Meccan except verses 17–33 and 48–50, and is commonly placed after al-ʿAlaq as the second revelation; despite ordering disputes it reflects the first revelation’s atmosphere.
rows.anchor: السورة مكية مبكرة، إلا آيات (17: 33، 48: 50) فمدنية

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Some say the surah, or most of it, was revealed about al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah and Abū Jahl ibn Hishām.
rows.anchor: وذكر بعضهم في أسباب نزولها أنها أو معظمها "في الوليد بن المغيرة المخزومي وأبى جهل بن هشام المخزومي

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: A proposed connection to the preceding surah says the opening clears the Prophet of accusations of madness, praises his patience and character, and answers the disbelievers’ claims of poetry and magic.
rows.anchor: فبدأ سبحانه وتعالى هذه السورة ببراءته مما كانوا ينسبونه إليه من الجنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says this coherence argument assumes muṣḥaf order: al-Mulk was revealed far later, around the seventy-seventh surah, over seventy revelations after al-Qalam.
rows.anchor: وفيه التفات إلى نسق هذا الترتيب، ولا يفوتنا معه أن سورة الملك نزلت متأخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ṣarīm means cut or harvested; reports also gloss it as black ash in Khuzayma speech or a known Yemeni sand.
rows.anchor: والصريم: المقطوع، والمحصود. ونقلوا أنه الرماد الأسود بلغة خزيمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent story is that the garden owners planned to harvest everything at dawn and leave nothing; the author rejects the gloss that they merely omitted saying in shāʾ Allāh.
rows.anchor: وظاهر النص، أن خطيئتهم التي أخذوا بها، هي التصميم على صرم جنتهم خفية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Takhāfut means whispering to one another so no one else hears the plan.
rows.anchor: والتخافت: أن يتحدث بعضهم إلى بعض في خفوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥard means withholding or preventing, with an added sense of aversion, as in a year withholding yield or a camel withholding milk.
rows.anchor: والحرد: المنع، من حردت السنة إذا منعت خيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Talāwum is reciprocal blame, each person blaming the others.
rows.anchor: والتلاوم: من صيغ المفاعلة، وذلك بأن يلوم بعضهم بعضاً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Awsat can mean just or equitable, evoking balance between two extremes.
rows.anchor: والعربية تستعمل الأوسط والوسط في معنى العدل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tasbīḥ here means remembering God, fulfilling His due, and thanking Him for His blessing.
rows.anchor: والتسبيح ذكر الله، ونفهمه في آية القلم: {لَوْلَا تُسَبِّحُونَ}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭughyān means exceeding bounds, first used of overflowing water and then of tyranny; this echoes the discussion of Pharaoh in al-Nāziʿāt.
rows.anchor: والطغيان: تجاوز الحد، وأصل استعماله في طغيان الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes elaborate the garden story: it belonged to a righteous man who left it to his people and town; reports place it in Yemen near Ṣanʿāʾ, Abyssinia, or among the People of Scripture.
rows.anchor: أن هذه الجنة كانت لرجل صالح، حدودا قومه وبلده فقيل إنه من أهل اليمن
